Nov 16, 2026 | Information and communication technologies, Theology

Domènec Melé, Emeritus Professor of the Chair of Business Ethics at IESE Business School-University of Navarra and emeritus member of the Royal European Academy of Doctors (READ), reflects on the impact of artificial intelligence and new technological environments on the spiritual development of human beings in the article “Christian Spirituality and Artificial Intelligence: Discernment in a Global Technological Economy”, published on 27 October in the journal Religions.

For the expert, artificial intelligence has shown that it not only expands human capabilities but also shapes habits, desires, attention and forms of relationship. However, he argues that processing information or generating plausible responses is not equivalent to wisdom, which requires integrating knowledge with experience, moral judgement and an orientation towards worthy ends. A fluid and personalised interaction may simulate attention or empathy, but it does not constitute communion, because communion requires reciprocal presence, vulnerability and the capacity for self-giving between persons, he states. In an economy that rewards engagement or productivity, Melé recalls that optimising means does not automatically determine which ends are worth pursuing.

These considerations, he adds, have practical consequences. AI can reduce repetitive burdens and broaden access to knowledge or assistance, but replacing activities whose value includes human participation — such as teaching, care, professional judgement or personal accompaniment — entails risks. There is also the danger of an unequal distribution of human presence, since those with greater resources may continue to have access to teachers, doctors or advisers in person, while others increasingly receive automated substitutes. The article also underlines the material footprint of technology. Although it may appear immaterial to users, artificial intelligence depends on data centres, chips and electricity grids whose consumption of energy and water is considerable.

Melé does not advocate rejecting technology, nor does he seek to absolutise it. Technical creativity can be understood as a form of participation in the care and development of creation, but the power it confers is a responsibility entrusted to human beings, not a form of absolute dominion. In a context of concentrated infrastructure, data and capital, he argues, the social doctrine of the Church offers criteria of dignity, the common good, subsidiarity and solidarity to prevent individuals and communities from becoming passive recipients of decisions taken elsewhere. Progress, he concludes, is genuinely human when it is directed towards the integral development of persons and, within the Christian horizon, towards communion with God and with others.

Over the past 30 years, Melé has researched and written extensively on business and economic ethics, corporate social responsibility, Christian social ethics, spirituality in management, management philosophy and humanistic management. He has published more than 70 book chapters and scientific articles in leading journals such as Journal of Business Ethics, Business Ethics Quarterly, Business Ethics: A European Review, Business and Society Review, Philosophy of Management and Humanistic Management Journal. He is also the author of several books that have become reference works in the field of humanistic economics, including “Ethics in Business Management”, “Anthropological Foundations of Business Management”, “Business Ethics in Action. Seeking Human Excellence in Organizations”, “Christians in Society” and “Ethics in the Family Business”, co-authored with fellow READ emeritus member Miguel Ángel Gallo.
